title: Using Modules
description: Bring in ready-made code from Python's built-in modules with import.

content.text: You don't build a hammer every time you need one. You grab the toolbox. Python comes with lots of ready-made toolboxes called **modules**, and `import` brings one into your program.

parts.label: tool
parts.note: The function you want from the toolbox.

parts.label: arguments
parts.note: What you hand to the tool, like any function.

content.value:
import random

dice = random.randint(1, 6)
print("You rolled a", dice)
content.caption: The number is random, so each run can print something different, like `You rolled a 4`.

content.value: Without the import line, the name `random` means nothing and Python stops with a `NameError`. Switch the import off in the explorer below to see exactly that.

content.question: What happens if you call `random.randint(1, 6)` without `import random`?
content.explain: Without the import, Python has never heard of `random`, so it stops with a `NameError`.

items.sub: A whole number from `a` to `b`, including both ends.
Picks one item out of a list.

content.title: For when a program shouldn't do the same thing every time

content.value:
import random

print(random.randint(1, 6))   # 1 to 6, either end possible
print(random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]))
content.caption: Random each time: for example `3` and then `paper`.

content.title: Look alike, behave differently
content.caption: `randint(1, 6)` includes 6, unlike `range(1, 6)`, which stops at 5. It's worth reading twice.

content.question: Which numbers can `random.randint(1, 3)` give?
content.explain: `randint` includes both ends, so 1, 2 and 3 are all possible.

items.sub: A stored value, not a function, so no parentheses.

content.title: The math module covers what the operators don't

steps.note: Load the `math` toolbox. Now the name `math` means something.
`sqrt` finds the square root. It always gives a float.
`pi` is a stored value, so there are no parentheses.
`floor` rounds down, even though 4.8 is close to 5.

content.value:
import math

print(math.sqrt(25))     # always a float
print(math.pi)
print(math.floor(4.8))   # rounded down

content.title: What time.sleep(1) does
content.caption: Handy for a countdown that appears one line at a time, instead of all at once.

content.value:
import time

print("Starting...")
time.sleep(1)
print("One second later!")
content.caption: The second line appears one second after the first.

content.question: What does `time.sleep(2)` do?
content.explain: `sleep` pauses the program for that many seconds. Then the next line runs as normal.

items.title: import module
items.text: Use the module name in front. A useful reminder of where a tool came from.

items.title: from module import tool
items.text: Pulls one tool out by name. Use it on its own, no `random.` in front.

content.title: Two ways to import
content.caption: The `from` form is shorter. Save it for the handful of tools you call constantly.

content.value:
from random import randint

print(randint(1, 6))   # no random. in front this time
content.caption: Random each time, a whole number from 1 to 6.

content.question: After `from math import sqrt`, which line works?
content.explain: `from math import sqrt` brings in just `sqrt`, so you use it on its own. The name `math` itself was not imported.

editorCode:
import random
import math

print("Dice roll:", random.randint(1, 6))
print("Pick one:", random.choice(["rock", "paper", "scissors"]))
print("Square root of 81:", math.sqrt(81))
print("Rounded down:", math.floor(9.7))

quiz.question: Which keyword brings a module into your program?
quiz.explain: import loads a ready-made module so you can use its tools without writing them yourself.

quiz.question: What happens if you call random.randint(1, 6) without importing random first?
quiz.explain: Until the import line runs, the name random does not exist, so Python has no idea what you are referring to.

quiz.question: Which of these can randint(1, 6) never return?
quiz.explain: randint includes both ends, so 1 and 6 are both possible. 0 is outside the range entirely.
